sources.title: Rong Hong / Yung Wing (Q1353934), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Yung Wing', description 'Chinese-American diplomat and businessman (1828-1912)', Chinese label 容閎, Korean label 용굉, instance of human, born 17 November 1828, died 21 April 1912, citizenship Qing dynasty and United States. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Edward J. M. Rhoads, Stepping Forth into the World: The Chinese Educational Mission to the United States, 1872-81 (Hong Kong University Press, 2011), publisher's free preview PDF (the parts that deal with Rong Hong were read: chapter 1 on the Mission's origins, the passages on recruitment and on the 1881 recall, and the notes and index). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: says the Mission was by nearly all accounts the brainchild of Yung Wing, sanctioned by the Qing court through his lobbying, the patronage of Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang and the Japanese example; says he was the first Chinese graduate of a Western university when he left Yale in 1854 (not the first Chinese to attend an American college, which was Zeng Laishun, and Huang Kuan graduated at Edinburgh a year later); gives the 1868 petition to Ding Richang, the 1870 Tianjin episode, Zeng's October 1870 memorial naming Chen Lanbin and Yung, the 1871 joint memorial for 120 boys, his recruiting in his home village, the nephews he sent to Monson Academy and the Mission, the 1881 recall, and how two students stayed on with the help of Leonard Bacon and Yung. Its notes record that a Chinese historian (Dong Shouyi) minimises Yung's role as originator and doubts his account of the four-point petition, and that his autobiography has other inaccuracies. Scholarly, archival and balanced; only the preview portions were read, not the later chapters on the students' careers.

Yung Wing, My Life in China and America (New York: Henry Holt and Company, 1909), Standard Ebooks edition of the Project Gutenberg text and the Internet Archive scan (University of Toronto copy); read in part: the passages on the declined comprador's post, the 1859 visit to the Taiping capital, the education scheme, the Peruvian commissioner and the coolie-trade investigation, the 1898 flight from Beijing and the 1901 interview with the governor of Formosa. SELF-ACCOUNT: the person's own memoir, written in old age and partly contested (a Chinese historian doubts his four-point petition); used only where another source also supports the claim, or where the row is capped at inference.

June Grasso, 'Yung Wing', EBSCO Research Starters, History (2024; read in full). Reference-article biography: poor peasant family near Macao, the Morrison Education Society school under Samuel R. Brown, Monson Academy 1847, Yale from 1850, naturalised 1852, graduated 1854; back in China in 1855 he worked as a translator and in his own trading enterprise; commissioned by Zeng Guofan in 1863 to buy machinery for the first modern arsenal; deputy to Chen Lanbin in the Mission from 1872; Chen's criticism of the students' Americanisation and of Yung's own way of life; the end of the Mission in 1881; support for the 1898 reform movement, flight, and a return to the United States in 1902. Draws on his memoir and on secondary studies, so it is not independent of them.

Ben Railton, 'Yung Wing, the Chinese Educational Mission, and Transnational Connecticut', ConnecticutHistory.org (CT Humanities, 2022; read in full). Interpretive essay by a literature professor that leans on the memoir: his refusal of a church group's offer that depended on a promise to become a missionary, his unaccepted offer to serve in the Union army, his marriage, the refusal of the first Annapolis and West Point entrants and the Chinese government's order to return, his bitter written comment on that refusal, and his return to Hartford in 1902.

Barbara Austen (Connecticut Historical Society), 'Yung Wing's Dream: The Chinese Educational Mission, 1872-1881', ConnecticutHistory.org (2021; read in full). Short archivist overview: 30 boys arrived in 1872, host families, the 1874 headquarters at 352 Collins Street in Hartford, the students' neglect of their Chinese studies, a recall in 1881 attributed to Americanisation, finances and a US breach of the Burlingame Treaty, and what the returnees went on to do.

Yale Council on East Asian Studies, 'Yung Wing' (read in full). Alma-mater page: first Chinese student to graduate from a North American university in 1854; choir, football and Boat Club at Yale; organised the Mission and sent 120 students; honorary doctorate of laws in 1876; gave more than 1,200 volumes in 1878 that became the core of Yale's East Asian library. Admiring institutional page.

MIT, 'Chinese Educational Mission', Early Chinese Students at MIT (read in full). Describes the Mission as the brainchild of Yung Wing, the 1872-1875 detachments, 43 students who entered college before the recall (Yale 20, MIT 8), MIT faculty protests against the 1881 recall, and returnees in the navy, mining, railways and telegraphy. Relies on Rhoads and LaFargue, so it is not independent of them.

Lian Xi, 'Returning to the Middle Kingdom: Yung Wing and the recalled students of the Chinese Educational Mission to the United States', Modern Asian Studies 49(1), 2015 (Cambridge Core page; ONLY THE ABSTRACT could be read, the full article is behind a paywall). Counter-voice on outcomes: argues that the recalled students met disillusion, marginalisation or co-option by the autocratic state and in the end failed to set China on a new modernising course. Not used as support for any row.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_memoir, src_rh_ebsco, src_rh_yale | 1863-1881 | scholarly history, memoir, reference biography, university page] Rhoads documents that by his own account he took his plan for sending students to the United States to a provincial governor in 1868, reminded him of it when the Tianjin crisis of 1870 brought him north, was named with Chen Lanbin to run the Mission, and travelled to his home village in the winter of 1871-72 to find the first boys; Rhoads and the reference biography also show him sent in 1863 to buy the arsenal machinery. A Chinese historian cited by Rhoads minimises his role as originator, so the originator claim is not scored on his word alone. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.62 to 70 / 0.58 because the four sources tell one story and two lean on his memoir. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 68 / 0.55 for outcome bias and the contested credit.

persistence.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_memoir, src_rh_ebsco | 1868-1902 | scholarly history, memoir, reference biography] The proposal he says he made in 1868 did not get a hearing for about two years (Rhoads); the Mission then ran nine years of a planned fifteen; after the 1881 recall he tried to keep the programme going and helped two students stay on (Rhoads); the reference biography and his memoir show him still pursuing reform after fleeing Beijing in 1898. The repeated return to the same aim is documented, but the later years rest on the reference biography and his memoir only. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.54. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 64 / 0.5 because the post-1898 activity is single-family.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_memoir, src_rh_yale, src_rh_ebsco | 1850-1881 | scholarly history, memoir, university page, reference biography] His stated aim, which Rhoads, MIT and Railton quote from his memoir, was that the rising generation of China should have the education he had had; conduct that fits it includes sending nephews to study in the United States (Rhoads says the eldest went to Monson Academy almost certainly at his instigation and expense, and another joined the Mission), his recruiting in his home village, his gift of more than 1,200 books to Yale in 1878 (Yale) and his refusal to work as a missionary or a comprador (Rhoads). The motive rests on his own statement; the actions are independently documented. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.62 to 70 / 0.56. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 68 / 0.52 because the stated motive is one self-quotation repeated by several pages.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_rh_memoir, src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_railton | 1850s | memoir, scholarly history, interpretive essay] He turned down church backers who wanted a promise that he would become a missionary and, back in China, turned down a comprador's post as servile, preferring to travel as the firm's agent or to translate independently (his memoir; Rhoads and Railton repeat it). Both episodes are his own account, restated rather than independently documented, and Rhoads says he found suitable work with difficulty at first. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.52 strong inference to 58 / 0.44 inference because every instance traces to the memoir; impact is dual-edged because the refusals left him struggling for work at first.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_memoir | 1868-1871 | scholarly history, memoir] Rhoads credits the Mission's approval to the combination of his lobbying with the patronage of Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, and relates that he won over Ding Richang, who then moved Zeng; but Zeng's memorial credits Ding rather than Yung with the idea, and a Chinese historian doubts his account of the petition. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.5 strong inference to 58 / 0.46 inference because the chain of persuasion is told from his own account and the credit is contested.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads | 1871-1881 | scholarly history] When the scholar-official class would not enrol its sons, Yung and the Shanghai merchant Xu Run used kinship and native-place ties to find candidates, and Yung went to his home village to ask relatives and friends; in 1881, with Leonard Bacon, he helped two recalled students, Tan Yaoxun and Rong Kui, find independent support so that they could stay in the United States. Two documented episodes, both from one scholar. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.56 to 64 / 0.52 because both come from a single scholar. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 62 / 0.5 because credit is shared with Xu Run and Bacon.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_memoir | 1870 | scholarly history, memoir] Rhoads says that when Governor Ding Richang took him north after the Tianjin massacre, Yung capitalised on the unexpected chance to remind him of the educational scheme, which Zeng Guofan then backed; Rhoads also credits Li Hongzhang, not Yung, with the argument from the Burlingame Treaty's education clause. A single episode. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.48 to 60 / 0.44 because it is one episode told from one chain of accounts.

adaptability.rationale: [src_rh_rhoads, src_rh_ebsco, src_rh_memoir | 1855-1902 | scholarly history, reference biography, memoir] Back in China in 1855 without a Confucian education he could not enter the civil service and refused missionary or comprador work; he became an independent tea trader and translator in Shanghai (Rhoads, reference biography), later joined Zeng Guofan's staff as a foreign-affairs expert, and after 1898 moved from Beijing to Shanghai to Hong Kong and back to the United States in 1902 (reference biography, memoir). Several career and place changes are documented, though the reasons are partly his own account. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.52 to 62 / 0.5. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 60 / 0.5 because forced exile is not the same as chosen adaptation.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_rh_memoir, src_rh_railton | 1873-1901 | memoir, interpretive essay] In his memoir he tells a Peruvian commissioner in Tianjin that he will oppose a labour treaty with Peru, and tells the Japanese governor of Formosa in 1901 that he wrote a mortgage proposal against Japan and would repeat it; Railton quotes his bitter written comment on the US treatment of the Mission. The two confrontations are self-told and no other source confirms them. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.46 to 58 / 0.42. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 56 / 0.4 because the episodes are self-reported anecdotes; impact is dual-edged.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: Stage B grade plausible (downgraded from strong, terms unread). Lead: the 1909 frontispiece of 'My Life in China and America'; LEAD SURVIVED, with the source swapped: instead of the Commons CC BY-SA 3.0 scan by Fred Hsu (a licence on the new scan, which adds nothing to the 1909 work) I cropped the frontispiece myself from the Internet Archive University of Toronto copy (item mylifeinchinaame00yunguoft, page n7, 2243 x 3469), whose record says 'Possible copyright status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT' and cites a visible 1909 copyright notice (US region); the UDL copy named in Stage B (mylifeinchinaand027665mbp) only has the legacy 'Copyrightowner: Henry Holt And Company' field and was not used. Sitter: the page carries a printed signature facsimile 'Very truly yours Yung Wing' and the facing title page names 'Yung Wing, A.B., LL.D. (Yale)'; I viewed both. Creator: unnamed; date: published 1909 (New York, Henry Holt), the sitter about 80. Holder terms: the live archive.org terms page is JavaScript-only; I read a 2022 Wayback capture of archive.org/about/terms.php: no fee or permission requirement, and users are responsible for rights (fair use / non-infringing use). Project Gutenberg #54635 was down for maintenance (not needed). KIND likeness. Quality: a 1909 halftone, 687 x 1000 after reduction, not upscaled. NAME: the frozen list and Wikipedia title use 'Rong Hong'; Western sources overwhelmingly say 'Yung Wing' (kept as the first alias, and used once in the editorial text); the lead may prefer 'Yung Wing' as the display name. REGION east_asia (Qing China; US citizenship also coded in nationality). KOREAN NAME 용굉 is the Wikidata ko label (no Korean Wikipedia article). CLASSIFICATION: occupations diplomat, educator; fields education, diplomacy; tags founder, organizer; archetypes institution_builder, organizational_leader. SCOPE: scoring is limited to conduct documented in the sources: the education scheme, his 1850s refusals, recruiting and the 1881 aftermath; his 1898-1902 reform activity is used only under persistence and adaptability. His role as originator is disputed in Chinese scholarship (Rhoads, note on Dong Shouyi), the memoir is partly unreliable, and Xi Lian's counter-reading of outcomes was available as an abstract only. READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Rhoads preview (relevant portions), memoir (parts), EBSCO Research Starters (full), Railton (full), Austen (full), Yale (full), MIT (full), Lian Xi (abstract only). Not read: Worthy 1965, Leibovitz and Miller 2011, LaFargue 1942, Hummel's Eminent Chinese (lending-restricted), the NYT obituary (bot wall), Rhoads chapters 2-11 beyond the preview. CONCENTRATION: nine rows, all lowered at the concentration step because CEM sources share one story and the memoir; autonomy_need and persuasiveness also moved from strong inference to inference. SELF-CALIBRATION lowered six rows further; raised 0. Sparse by design; eligibility_v2 is a separate diagnostic and was not a target.
